utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Thursday, and I welcome our witness. Then I also greet Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic, and, of course, Mr. Coric also. I welcome the Defence counsels, Mr. Kruger, Mr. Stringer, and their case manager, and everyone helping us. We will resume. Mr. Kruger has 20 minutes left. But I first need to give the floor to the Registrar for some IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Stojic Defence has submitted their objections to the list of documents tendered for admission by 3D through Witness Slobodan Praljak. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1064. The Petkovic Defence has also submitted their response to the Prosecution objections to documents tendered through Witness Zvonimir Skender. This list shall be given Exhibit IC1065. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Registrar. Before giving the floor to Mr. Kruger, I have two questions to put after the documents we'd seen yesterday. You know that a good night's sleep is excellent, and overnight I've thought about a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the first document, could the Registrar please put document 3D00796, the document we saw yesterday. We have the document on the screen now. Witness, please, could you please read the document in your own language. Read out loud the third paragraph, please, or read the third paragraph. I don't know if it's out loud or not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read out loud, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third paragraph of this document, starting with "na sastanku," something like that. Please read it out loud. Read it out loud so that the interpreters can translate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Paragraph 3 or item 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking you to read the bullet point number 3. I would like you to read the third paragraph from the beginning of the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The following conclusions have been unanimously adopted at the meeting, precisely the demands of the Government of the HR-HB, as well as these of Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence counsel, and municipal governments and political structures within the HR-HB."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I asked you to read this paragraph out loud because yesterday the Prosecutor focused on the fact that this letter had been sent to Mate Boban, Mate Boban, the minister of defence and the commander of the HVO, but he did not mention the fact that the municipal governments also received this letter. Witness, could you please tell us why you thought it was also useful to inform the governments of municipalities of these problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we thought that the municipal government were controlling substantial economic and financial resources that could considerably improve the material status of the soldiers deployed in our units and could partly reassure the mobilisation of resources in the possession of either citizens or socially-owned or state-owned work organisations, as they used to be called at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, at the end of the document, you will note that the municipal government were not in copy of this document. Is it because they were forgotten to be placed on the CC list or was it deliberate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as a brigade commander was present at the meeting, I endorsed these conclusions. However, as for the process of dispatching this document, it was not up to me to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question. Could the Registrar please display Exhibit P01653. It's a document you wrote on March 11, 1993. Witness, could you please read out loud the beginning of the first paragraph, and read it slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours: "Having realised what happened on the territory of our mother country Croatia during the war against the Serb Chetnik armada, the Croatian population in the area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna organised themselves and made preparations for the defence of their territory."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can stop here. So you are writing, at least in your own words: "Having realised what happened on the territory of our mother country Croatia ..." So there's something I don't understand here. Gornji Vakuf is part and parcel of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so any simple mind would draw the following conclusion: When you live in Gornji Vakuf, your mother country is the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but you are writing the mother country, the homeland, is Croatia. So the same simple mind could very -- infer from this that what you're writing, actually, is that the municipality of Gornji Vakuf is attached to Croatia as its homeland. So could you please explain what you meant? Did you just make an error when you were writing or did you write this without paying attention? What exactly did you mean when you wrote this, because these are your own words. I believe you drafted it, unless one of your officers drafted it for you and you just signed it. I don't know. So what does this sentence mean? What do you mean when you say "our motherland, Croatia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we simply recognised the fact that both Croatia and the BH were proclaimed independent states after the break-up of Yugoslavia. The majority of Croats, no matter where they were living in, in the US, here in the Netherlands, or in Bosnia-Herzegovina, saw the state of Croatia to be as their own state as well. Being aware that I was a resident of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that I have dual citizenship of both the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, I can rightly call both these states my homeland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understand what you said. What you're telling us is the following: As a Croat, whether you live in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Netherlands, in the US, or anywhere, you remain a Croat, and your mother country is Croatia, which is why you're telling us that you have dual citizenship. Did I sum up your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have summed it up very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This helps understand how to interpret this paragraph, because I hadn't really caught that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As Judges started with questions, I would like to come back also to the previous document, 3D00796. You don't actually need the document to answer my question. What strikes me with this document is the very fact that commanders meet amongst themselves, discuss common problems, and then address a letter with the result of their discussion to authorities. In my experience with the military, this is very unusual. The normal thing would be that such issues are discussed in the presence and under the direction of the commander of the army, which at that point, I think, was Mr. Praljak, the accused Praljak. I hesitate about an explanation. One possibility is that it denotes the fact that your commanders did this with the exclusion of your boss, betrays a certain lack of confidence in the commander, but that might be completely wrong. I would like you to explain. How come this was the method used by commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I agree that this is not the usual method of communication between commanders and the civilian authorities, but one has to bear in mind the context of the time when this was being written. The BH forces were mounting offensive activities, and we were facing considerable problems on all defence lines. Due to that, we requested additional actions and measures to be undertaken that would ensure that we have full strength of manpower, that we have financial and material means at our disposal, so as to enable us to carry out our defence tasks of the territory and the Croatian population that we were entrusted as part of our mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have not addressed what was my main query. Why is General Praljak absent in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you may have noticed in the letterhead this has to do with the North-Western Herzegovina Operation Zone and brigade commanders from that particular area of responsibility, so this is one level lower beyond or below the Main Staff. And for that reason, the commander of the Main Staff was not included. However, he was supposed to receive both the letter and the conclusions that were reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yet the normal line of command would be that you address the general, and the general then would deal with civil authorities, yet you have bypassed him. If I say "you," I do not mean Mr. Tokic. I mean the group of commanders; Mr. Siljeg, I think, in the first place. Why not go the normal way via the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in wartime commanders come to briefing sessions, and this took place after the working meeting or the daily briefing were finished. All these officers attended the working briefing session that took place after they discharged their daily duties. This happened most often at around 8.00 or 9.00 p.m. So to shift the officers around in order to convene some themed meetings during the offensive that is being carried out by the BH Army forces would be foolish and would put us at risk by not being where the focus of our task was, and that was to defend the territory in which we were commanding our units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This, in my understanding, does not explain why you did not seize, with this letter, your commander, whose task it would then have been to deal with the civil authorities, but I will not insist. If you want to add something, you're welcome. If not, the floor is to Mr. Kruger of the.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, I'd like to follow up on what my fellow Judge just asked. I also have some experience in military business because I went through the Military Academy for one year, so I am fairly versed in military matters. We've already studied this document with another witness, and I had also asked this other witness the same questions that my fellow Judge just put to you. I wondered at the time whether this document didn't reveal a couple of things; first, that there was unease within the HVO, within the army of the HVO, where the chain of command was actually challenged, or whether this -- rather, given all the topics addressed in this document, wouldn't it be sort of a quasi-putsch of the commanders of operational zones who are showing their hierarchy that they don't agree on a number of points? So any Judge must wonder, when looking at this document and when placing this document back in the context of all the other evidence heard, a Judge must absolutely wonder why in this document you've got a list of everything that needs to be done, even though Mr. Praljak is absent from this meeting, and the fact that this document is sent to Mr. Praljak as well as to his superiors. So we would really like to know whether this document doesn't demonstrate that the policy and the measures implemented and triggered by Mate Boban is being challenged. So you were there, you discussed all this with your colleagues, you signed the document, so you have a point of view. Were you happy with the way things were going? But if that's the case, why write this document? And if you were unhappy, then maybe there was a reason for this document that you could tell us about. So what's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document does not challenge the chain of command in any way whatsoever. When writing this document, we were thinking as commanders do, and that is that we should highlight certain problems, because we, as commanders, were not responsible for that and were not authorised to deal with these issues. The situation was such that the municipality of Bugojno had fallen, including part of Novi Travnik, Fojnica, and parts towards Uskoplje, and that the BH Army forces from these areas were exerting pressure on the HVO, so we were simply supposed to put aside or just forget about any comfortable living outside of the war zones and that we should mobilise all our efforts and forces to effect the defence. That was the fundamental premise on which we, the commanders, worked when we drafted this appeal, but at the same time we were prepared, with the forces that we had at the disposal, to carry out any task given to us by the Main Staff and President Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood correctly, you were calling out for help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour -- [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. I wouldn't like to intervene, but I gather, from your questions, how much importance you attach to this document. Therefore, every word uttered by this witness is equally important. In that context, towards the end of this answer, the witness said that this meeting was a cry for help addressed to higher instances. This word "cry for help" is the key word. Originally, it has been translated as an appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kovacic. What are you doing, commenting on what the witness says, explaining the document? I think that's what you are doing, and that's not correct, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm now really confused. I don't understand why you are attacking me. I'm simply discussing the word, the translation. The witness said "vapaj," and I'm kindly asking the interpreters to interpret. It was translated as "appeal." It is general, it is not "vapaj." The Croatian word "vapaj," I'm kindly asking the interpreters to translate what does it mean. This is a cry for help. As I see, it is now -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I may have mis-reacted. Please do not take it against me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I'm sure you understood -- you found out that I had noticed this, because in my answer [as interpreted] I said this document is a cry for help, and my question actually said, In this document, you were calling out for help? And the witness, on the transcript, answered by saying, That is correct. No need to worry. I had preempted all this. But you are right. In the English translation, the word was "appeal," which is a bit different from "cry for help." So you're right to point this out. But I had noticed it, which is why I put it in my question, in my summary question, Was this a cry for help?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Precisely because of that, I went back to this portion because I understood that it was a significant thought and that it must be recorded in the transcript. You obviously thought the same and raised the question. I apologise to Judge Trechsel once again, but I wasn't sure what we were talking about, so I thought it might be due to the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I? When I was asking a question to the witness, I noticed that Mr. Praljak very loudly - I could hear it also - communicated with counsel. What did you say, Mr. Praljak? Do you remember? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do remember. The question about this meeting, how the meeting came into being, at whose initiative, and whether I was there, and on page 70, line 21-29 [as interpreted] on 2009, there was a question there, and I told counsel to find these facts and information so that I could ask him what he's already said or, rather, whether he agrees with what he's already said, because I don't think he fully understood the intentions and the lines of which your question was asked, and then to refer to the transcript. So I asked counsel to provide me with the page of the transcript, the page number, and the witness's answer to the question of who initiated the meeting, who convened the meeting, and whether I attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can understand that there is a problem with communication between client and counsel in this room. You do it normally with little paper slips, and it is not always correct. But it is not -- it is not correct at all to do it in the way you did it because you -- the witness can also hear it, and there is then a danger that he may be in some way influenced. I just would invite you not to do this again, and close the debate on this issue therewith. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, Judge Trechsel. I didn't mention any information to counsel. I just asked for the number, the page number where the question was asked. And, secondly, we use -- well, the guards can't -- aren't allowed to take notes to counsel. Counsel can't get up and send notes. So I can't keep sending the Pusic Defence on errands like that. It's not my fault that the courtroom functions in that way. I didn't mention any other piece of information. I just wanted to know what page in the transcript the question was asked on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the rights of the Defence hadn't escaped me. During the break, I had asked the Registrar whether the accused would be entitled to sit next to their counsel, like it is the case in the USA, but for security reasons I was told that it was not possible. Since nobody has called this into question, I had tried to find a solution that would be acceptable to all. Now, if you want to communicate, if you send small slips of paper, your counsel can then respond likewise. If, at the inception of this Tribunal, people had thought about what criminal cases are all about, the accused would have sat next to their counsel, like that is the case in a great number of countries, where the lawyers can talk to their clients. If you look at the videos and the films on Nuremberg, the accused could talk to their counsel directly, but these were other times, Mr. Praljak. And we shall close the debate on this issue now. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could have someone to fetch and carry those notes, because I can't keep asking Defence counsel from another Defence team to ask them to carry our notes in the courtroom. The guards aren't allowed to do this, and it's really become a big problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the Registrar is keeping track in realtime of everything that is going on, I'm sure the Registry will tell us what the best way of easing the communication between counsel and accused will be, since there are a number of people working in the Registry. And since these are all smart people, I'm sure they will come up with a workable solution. Mr. Kruger, you have 20 minutes left. We have spent a lot of time on these matters, but it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokic, good morning to you. We only have 20 minutes. I'm going to show four documents to you, maybe a fifth one. The first topic is just going to conclude with a topic that we've already been discussing this morning. If you can go, from where you are in your binder, three documents further on; that is, document P03475, P03475. Now, sir, this document, dated the 15th of July, 1993, is from you, as Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade commander, and by Mr. Zvonko Katovic, chief of SIS. What I'd like to ask you about is, if you look at the list of addressees at the top, this is addressed to the HZ-HB Defence Department, personally to Mr. Bruno Stojic, Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, Mr. Mate Boban, Mr. Jadranko Prlic. Now, sir, the only question I have on this: The fact that you've addressed this communication to these persons, three of which are in the courtroom today, you did that because you recognised these people as your leader. You, as an HVO Brigade commander, they were your leaders?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, I thought that the people responsible were those who could make good-quality decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, let's turn two documents previously, two documents before the document you're looking at now, I think it's two, and that is document P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have just looked at the document in your language because I also look at the documents in your language. We talk about an order here. Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Boban, Mr. Prlic. Was this an order which you wanted to convey or was this done by chance? Had I been Mr. Boban, I wouldn't have been happy about this, because if I were Mate Boban at the head of the armed forces, to be on the list after Mr. Petkovic, well, this would have been a problem for me. Did you know nothing about these people's positions? Was this just a random order, or if there is any logic behind it, what kind of logic is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document was compiled by a security officer, and I have to mention, in this regard, how this document came into being, the reason for it being written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're not answering my question. You are giving me the reasons. What I would like to know is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I knew the disposition and positions within the authorities in the HR-HB, and as to the order of the addressees, I said that this was done by the Security Service, and I agreed to sending Vinko Zuljevic away from this area or, rather, to leave him in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that you were not the person who prepared the document. That satisfies me. Thank you. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can turn to document P02486, and it's the document two documents prior to the one we've just looked at. P024 -- no. Before, sir, to the front of your -- thank you, Mr. Usher. If you can find the original version. There you go. Now, sir, this is a letter dated the 22nd of May, 1993. It's "Top secret, confidential." Subject: "Delivery of information in reference to your letter of 19 of May." Now, if you look at the end of the document, we see that it's signed by the commander of the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade. And is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just to orient us all to what this is about, if we look, and this is in the English version on page 2, and in the original version it's -- in the B/C/S version, it's the last page, about 11 lines from the top, and it says: "Mr. Ante Kartalic was sent to Germany and other West European countries as an envoy of our brigade and the HVO. His mission is to witness the session of the clubs and pass them the latest information related to events in Gornji Vakuf as well as in our border area ." Sir, is it correct that this letter was provided to Mr. Ante Kartalic and this was basically addressed to the club of Croats in Stuttgart to inform them of events in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the very first paragraph of the letter, it says that: "The Croat population has been waging a war against the Serbs for quite some time and has been at war with Muslim forces during the past several months." And then what I'd like to ask you about: "The aim of the war is clear to us, who are in the command of the brigade, as well as to our soldiers in the brigade. That aim is to defend the existence of Croat people in this area, to defend material goods owned by the Croat people, to fight for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or a province with a Croatian prefix, which we are certainly going to achieve either by political or by military-type actions. We must not give up these sacred goals ... I'm afraid that this kind of historic opportunity won't be given to us again." Sir, the thoughts that you're expressing here, they're not your own ideas; these thoughts are in line with the thoughts of the leadership of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this document was compiled in the command and headquarters of the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade and quite simply reflects my opinion, as the commander, and the officers who helped to conceive this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. But if you talk about "our" or "these sacred goals," these aren't just your goals; these are the goals of the Bosnian Croat people and as developed by your leadership?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I repeat, these are the words which I, together with the command, compiled. Now, I don't know what the concept and platform of the leadership of the Croatian Community of the HR-HB was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, if we go down, then, further, it says, and this is about in the middle of page 1 in the English version, and it's the same paragraph further way down: "It doesn't matter to us whether our victory will be accomplished in political or military way, but it will largely depend on the choice of the Muslim side." Now, sir, this is the second time that you refer, in this communication, that the goals, the sacred goals, will be achieved either through military means or through military means. Is it correct, sir, that if the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, which you knew about, was implemented, that would have achieved those goals via the political means; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But, sir, isn't it so that you had mentioned that you knew that Gornji Vakuf was supposed to be included within the HZ-HB, and if we look at the province -- provinces of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, that would basically have entailed the same thing; Gornji Vakuf would have been included in the territory assigned to the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that through the Vance-Owen Plan, Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje was supposed to be within the territory where there was a majority Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, but you were thinking of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, because just about two lines below that, it says: "The events that took place in Gornji Vakuf from 13 May to 16 May 1993 clearly show that the Muslims are not content with the political option offered in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan" or "Vance-Owen's plan." So, sir, yesterday you already told us that the Muslims in Gornji Vakuf weren't pleased with the inclusion of Gornji Vakuf in the HZ-HB. Here you admit or you say they are not pleased with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, so, sir, that only leaves the military option over to achieve the sacred goals that you're referring to; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, no, that is not correct. In addition to the Vance-Owen Plan, there were other plans, and political negotiations continued. Under all the conditions and circumstances, the final instance is resorting to having the military solve the problem. And yesterday I said that most of the Muslims in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje did not accept the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that from this letter, we can see that your attitude, and I put it to you that this is not just your attitude, this is the attitude of the HVO at large, was that the sacred goals of the Bosnian Croats was the only thing that mattered, and what the Muslims wanted or desired didn't matter, and you would push through your will, the Bosnian Croat will, at all costs. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely incorrect, because everything I did, as a brigade commander, I did quite simply -- well, I did everything to prevent a conflict, to give enough space to the politicians to decide upon the setup and organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's step off this topic. I'd first like to show you a further document just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I cut in?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. I just would like to make an observation regarding the translation of the document. In the first line, we read the expression "Croatian province Herceg-Bosna," which struck me, but I think it is Croatian unity, it is nothing else than HZ-HB; is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the original document, Your Honour, it said "Hrvatska Zajednica," "Croatian Community."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have read this letter. I have listened to the questions put by the Prosecutor. First of all, your letter dated the 22nd of May answers the letter of the 19th of May, 1993, which we don't have. Since I don't have this letter, I find it difficult to interpret your letter, since I don't have the original letter dated the 19th of May. That said, I realise that you describe the situation in your letter, and then at the end of the letter you address the following fact: You explain that the brigade has sent Ante Kartalic to tour the clubs, whether they be in Stuttgart or in Austria or in Switzerland, for what reason? You explain in the letter that there are people working abroad who have not returned to come and fight, and you say since the 1st of January, 1992, they can be considered to be deserters and proceedings can be initiated against them. This is written in the document. In addition, you add that the list of these deserters could be published in newspapers. So these Croatian workers abroad have been told what their status is quite clearly. These are deserters. And then you continue and you say the salaries are not being paid out, if the people who don't get their salaries are unhappy and morale is low, we need 100 Deutchemarks for a T-55, and you total this, and you say what is needed is 1.450.000 Deutchemark. So on looking at this letter, what I feel is this: Wasn't it with a view to collecting funds, a form of racketeering to bring money back into the country? We have heard witnesses. We have seen evidence which indicated that the military budgets at the time was being set up, that aid money was coming in from the Croats who were sending money in. We have a lot of proof for this. Despite this and despite the system set up by the HVO, a brigade commander sends somebody to go and collect some funds. So it -- was this attitude approved by the civilian authorities of the HVO, who would have encouraged you to do this, or was this something that you did on your own bat, for whatever reason you decided to bring some money back into the country, because you felt somewhat autonomous vis-a-vis the HVO? Can you explain to me what the purpose of this letter is? The Prosecutor has his view on the letter. On looking at the purpose of this letter, I see that it has to do with money matters. Can you explain to us what this is about, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I will explain. The HVO -- the local HVO and, later on, the Croatian government -- when I say "Croatian government," I mean the Croatian Republic in Herceg-Bosna, introduced a requirement by which workers, working abroad, should give contributions, who had permanent work permits abroad from the 1st of January, 1992. So that applied to that population. And if I remember correctly it was to the tune of 300 German marks, a one-time donation, and this applied to all the countries of Western Europe where there were Croatian guest workers. And this responsibility and duty was implemented by the local HVO. Clubs were formed in Western Europe, and the monies were collected in those clubs, and then the money was forwarded to the local HVO right up until the time when, for reasons unknown to me, they -- there was an argument that broke out as to who was responsible for this and who would be given the money. The situation culminated in an event which took place in Mannheim, when a group of HVO representatives arrived in Germany, took over the money, and set out for Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje. Somebody called from Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje, and the president of the Mannheim club came to the railway station and asked that the money be returned. The gentleman who took the money returned the money. After that, having reached an agreement with the HVO, my assistant for security went out into the field. His name was Zvonko Katovic, that is to say, he went to -- he travelled to Germany and Austria, as well as Mr. Ante Kartalic, and all this was agreed with Mr. Ivan Saric, and they were given the possibility for those financial resources to go to the brigade treasury directly and to be used to pay out the salaries and to improve the material conditions and circumstances of the brigade. And it is for those reasons -- and by way of a proclamation, it was asked that everybody working without the official papers and had fled to Western countries should either come back home and join or place themselves at the disposal of the HVO, because otherwise they would be considered deserters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me stop you here because your answer is very lengthy. But in a nutshell, according to you, at the local level in Gornji Vakuf in the municipality, you're talking about Mr. Saric and the commander of the brigade, you had to get money because you needed money? Basically, that's your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right, because the people in Germany organised themselves and they were willing to send the money for defence in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, these clubs, were they clubs of Croats from Gornji Vakuf or generally clubs of Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In most cases, those were Croat clubs, but they were not strictly linked to the Croats from Gornji Vakuf. It gathered Croats working in Stuttgart, Vienna, and other European cities. If we appealed to them, then we would most often ask the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: How, if you know, did other brigades react? It looks to me a bit like you went to a pot of cream, which was cream for all Croats, and you took -- there, you tried to get as much as you could for you, your brigade being a relatively small part of the whole defence effort. It's not a problem that is addressed by the indictment, I accept, but it's an ethical question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you may have noticed yesterday the document which says that around 1.100 people had permanent working permits from Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje abroad, and those were the people on whom we were concentrated most. But all other people of goodwill provided money and -- for raising the funds. The other brigades had a much more widespread diaspora. I will mention that only Livno has 40.000 emigres and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Tomislavgrad has 40.000 emigres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and Livno had 30.000 emigres, so -- and they live in European countries and other countries outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, both Tomislavgrad and Livno were able to raise considerably more funds than we.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I would like to draw your attention that the witness is talking about document 56017, and it's P61 -- 56 -- P6017, P6017.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know how it's recorded correctly. The witness said "Saric," and I heard in my headphones "Coric," and I think this mistake should be rectified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did say "Saric." Coric has nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I think we have time for two more documents. If you go forward in your binder two documents, you will find document P01433 earlier in your binder. Do you have the document? P01433. Now, sir, all that I want to point to you -- point out to you in this document, it's by Mr. Mile Curic on the 7th of February to the HVO Mostar Main Staff and the operational zone -- or the Zone of Operations Tomislavgrad. It's a regular combat report. The only thing I draw your attention to is, in the second paragraph, the second-last sentence, it says: "Our side continued to burn buildings, Uzricje, Zdrimci, Dusa, Kupra." Now, I'd like you to bear that in mind for our next topic, and for that I want you to turn to just the document in front of this one, which is document P01351. Just in front of that document, P01351. Now, before looking at the document, in your statement, on page 12 in the English version, and you needn't look at it, but you refer there, and this relates to the end of January 1993 in Gornji Vakuf: "I recall there was one commission whose purpose was to establish how many tractors or cars was a person missing." Do you recall that there was such a commission established at the end of January in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This commission was set up on the UNPROFOR base in Gornji Vakuf, and it was supposed to visit the whole area where combat operations were being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with that, let's look at the document which is a document by Mr. Zeljko Siljeg of the 28th of January, 1993, and it's the report on the situation in Gornji Vakuf on January 28, 1993. And interesting to note, once again, the persons who this is addressed to, the Presidency of the HVO of the HZ-HB, the Government of the HVO HZ-HB Mostar, the Defence Department of the HVO HZ-HB Mostar, and the General Staff of the HVO HZ-HB Mostar. But let's turn in this document, which we've looked at before during your testimony, and we'll turn to page 3 of the English version, and in the B/C/S version it is the second page, and the first half of the page: This relates to the record of the commission in establishing the factual state on the occasion of combat operations on the terrain Uzricje, Duse, Trnovaca, Luzani, and Gornja Ricica, and it starts with a report on Uzricje. And if we look at what this -- what the commission, or sub-commission, as it's referred to, has recorded, it says, for Uzricje -- and if you turn to item 5, it says: "Looted two tractors and luxury cars." But just in front of that, item four, it says: "A total of 24 houses was destroyed (22 torched and 2 shelled)." And that's correct, isn't is it? In Uzricje, there was quite a destruction of houses? You don't dispute this?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but these were Croatian. However, for the most part, they were Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's go a little bit further. I will discuss that in a moment. And let's look at what it says for Dusa. Dusa, it's page 3 at the top in the B/C/S version, and in the English version, if we turn to page 5, right at the bottom, it says a total of 18 houses and sheds were destroyed, of which 16 were torched and two houses were destroyed by shelling. And if we turn to Trnovaca, just the next item, this says that a total of four houses were destroyed or torched. Now, sir, all that I want to put to you here is: Isn't is it correct, despite what you've just said now, that the majority of houses that were destroyed in these villages was, in the first place, destroyed by torching and not shelling?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the majority of houses were destroyed by fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, this Court has heard evidence that the bulk of this torching occurred after these villages had been taken over by the HVO, in actual fact; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I should say that two-thirds of the houses were devastated or destroyed after the military operations were over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, isn't it also correct that the bulk of the properties that were destroyed in these villages were actually Muslim properties?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said so, the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, if we can turn to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, you have to finish because you're running out of time. One last question, one last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, if I may finish on this document. It's nearly finished. If we, on the same document, turn to page 7 of the English, and, it's in the B/C/S, page 3, towards the bottom. And here it reports that some crimes are being reported; and I'll just refer you to: "They have no arguments for them, and they want the following cases to be investigated." I suppose that this is that the -- the Muslim side wants the following cases to be investigated. First: "Pavo Posavac, from the village of Duse, allegedly fired from a recoilless gun on the house of Enver Sljivo, in which his wife and children were killed. "I have already referred to the case of Branko Sapina." And then it's reported the case of Vlatko Rajic, who we've of heard previously, decapitated a Muslim, and then it ends with: "Rezo mistreated prisoners in Trnovaca." Sir, here we have crimes being reported, and these crimes are being reported right up to the very top of the HVO pyramid leadership structure. My question is: What came -- what became of this? Were these crimes investigated? We know about Vlatko Rajic, but what about these others? What happened?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we have here listed the names of people who in any way could not have been involved in any acts barred by the international law. Let's start with Ivan Saric, the president of HVO and HDZ. He was a civilian who was not involved in any acts. Ivan Kraljevic was my assistant for propaganda and information. Pero Mejdandzic was my assistant for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I could --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slowly give us the names and the function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I may interrupt you. I'm sorry. The basic question is: Were there any investigations or prosecutions which came out of this request for these cases to be investigated?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For all those individuals for whom it had been established that had maltreated prisoners, my assistant for security, in cooperation with the military police, launched an investigation. As for the men I just listed, it has never been established that they did anything in violation of the International Laws of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask one question on just the Trnovaca issue? It's literally one question, and then I am finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead if it's your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the last incident mentioned refers to a prisoner in Trnovaca. In your statement, you mentioned that 217 detained prisoners were held in a Trnovaca furniture factory, and these were being held, I take it, by the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade. My question to you, the last one, is: Once your HVO -- or members of your HVO unit had taken these people into custody, was it also your responsibility or the HVO military's responsibility to feed these people while they were in your custody?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the soldiers or military conscripts captured by the HVO were secured in accordance with what was available to us, and we also provided shelter with running water, and we also provided food, but it all depended on the resources that we had available. Therefore, we took care of all the people in custody. And I would like to note that at the time in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje, there was no electricity. Neither the Croats, nor the Bosniak, nor my soldiers had ideal conditions for personal hygiene and other necessities and needs, for the reasons that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So from what you're saying, it was your responsibility to take care of these people once they were in your custody?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Through the Home Guard Battalion, our brigade undertook obligation to provide proper shelter and accommodation for these people in the facilities around the factory of furniture for civilians and for soldiers inside the factory and inside the cafeteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions. Sorry for running over a few minutes, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, redirect. We know that Mr. Kovacic and Ms. Alaburic have questions. This will be deducted, of course. The only question is the time for Mr. Kovacic. Will you take this on your own time credit or on Mr. Petkovic's time credit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On your own time. Very well, then, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are going to start before the break, I would first like to give the floor to Mr. Praljak, who has a couple of questions. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we only have seven minutes before the break, and I will take more than seven minutes, so therefore I would prefer that we first go on break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Further cross-examination by Mr. Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tokic.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let us just try to clarify a few things. The meeting of the 26th of October, 1993, in the first part I asked you, and that's on page 70, line 21, whether this meeting was agreed during previous discussions and was it me who initiated this meeting. You responded by saying, Yes. Do you stand by your statement, and do you rely on your memory about who initiated it?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my statement that you, General, were the one who initiated this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My second question is: Do you recall that at the briefing about the military issues that preceded this meeting, that I was at that meeting as well?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: A few questions why this meeting, that you qualified as a cry for help, was necessary. Tell me, when was it that the BH Army attacked the HVO in Bugojno and captured the town, with all the consequences that stemmed from that?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, as far as I can remember, that took place in early July, but I think that Bugojno finally fell on the 12th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, right away, prior to that moment, were the relations between the HVO and ABiH in Bugojno were at an enviable level; there were no clashes and no conflicts, at a relatively enviable level?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were proud of their relationship, and they said that all the others should follow their example and maintain this kind of a communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the HVO of Bugojno, in view of such relationships, was preparing itself for any possible attack by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It seems I have to recall all the time the same things. Wait after Mr. Praljak has ended his question, because the interpreters have not yet finished translating. Then start speaking. Otherwise, you overlap and it's very difficult for the interpreters to do their job. Please start your answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. General, the Bugojno HVO was totally unprepared for an attack by the ABiH, and for that reason Bugojno fell in such a short time. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After this event, the ABiH, did they launch an attack along the axis Uskoplje-Rama and further on? From that moment on, were the ABiH in your area launching offensives in that region?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, the ABiH attacked HVO units on the 24th of June, 1993, in the area of the village of Voljice, micro-location Kute, and their task was to take control of Podravina, and from that moment on the conflict in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje started and continued until the signing of the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you and your brigade in that period ever have rotation on lines or were all your soldiers compelled to be in the trenches and on the lines all the time, without the possibility of a replacement?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this last clash, the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade, from June until February 1994, was constantly on the line without any possibility for my troops to be rotated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: After such long tours of service, do you know if your soldiers were totally physically and mentally exhausted?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My soldiers were both physically and mentally exhausted, and I might even say that they wished to sustain some slight injuries in order to shorten their stay on the battle-field at Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: From the moment that I arrived up there as commander of the Main Staff, and we've already discussed that and established that, did I force you to go to the front-line and to fight most of your time as brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, as brigade commander I had to set an example and I had to lead the soldiers in the execution of their duties, which meant that I had to be up at the front-line all the time, and not infrequently I held the line and positions with -- together with my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollections, what about Siljeg; did he take his whole command, the command of the operative zone, and did he have to go to the front-line as well, in view of the number of men that we had at our disposal?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, because there was a general shortage of manpower up at the front-line on the Uskoplje front, the Command of North-West Herzegovina and the Tomislavgrad Operative Zone had to hold our positions at Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know that I did that too?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, you did not at all answer the previous question, which related to Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did say that the Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina, whose commander was Siljeg, together with the command, held our defence lines at Crni Vrh. So Colonel Siljeg, but Colonel Siljeg was not up at the front-line. However, most of the command was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an answer. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, please, how many dead and wounded your brigade had during the war.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, the Dr. Ante Starcevic Brigade, from the beginning of the war, that is to say, from 1992, up until the end of the war, suffered casualties to the tune of 149 dead and 406 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Faced with a situation like that, was it -- was one of the basic problems that you faced with the soldiers the question of deserters? Was that a fundamental problem that you were confronted with?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the basic problems was the replenishment of troops, and so the people who fled and whom we called deserters, for the simple reason that they'd fled from their units and thereby avoided carrying out their assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did they flee to Croatia, and did they flee abroad?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly to Croatia or to other countries of Western Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning. This doesn't really seem to be questions that comes from any cross-examination. This is just taking up new --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, to make sure that you don't run into any problems, and you started correctly because you quoted some page numbers and line numbers, but you should say, During the cross-examination, you said this or that to the Prosecutor, and I would like to put a few questions to you regarding your answers. Now, as to the question of the deserters, we already mentioned it. You should have recalled that it had been mentioned during the cross-examination. Ms. Alaburic. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I do remember that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the page number which I can give you. In yesterday's transcript, on page 11, the Stojic Defence question about deserters was recorded, and what the brigade command could do and what anybody else could possibly do. So that was a topic that was broached and prepared by the Petkovic Defence as well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I did not include anything that was not mentioned in the cross-examination, but I will refer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Judge Antonetti asked about deserters, and you asked the following, Your Honour: Did you consider deserters to be those Croats in Germany who were normally working there, temporarily employed abroad, as was the euphemism and term used for people who had left earlier, or did you consider deserters to be only those who, after the beginning of the conflict, fled in order to avoid their military duties?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, deserters are people who fled when the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina began and who simply fled from their units or from the territory of Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje, whereas workers who found themselves abroad, working abroad, before the conflict broke out were not considered to be deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back in time. The document is 4D01667. You don't have to look at the document, but I'm just referring to that. The 5th Column is mentioned in that document, and you were asked by Judge Antonetti, on page 20-18 to 25, something about the 5th Column. Tell us, please, Mr. Tokic, after the JNA aggression started and the aggression by the Army of Republika Srpska, on the ground were there people who had previously been included in the various intelligence services and secret services of the former Yugoslavia, and did they disseminate all manner of rumours; for example, who was fighting -- who was against who, who was preparing to attack whom, what kind of characteristics one man had and another man had, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, we had to take care of this kind of activity all the time, people who wanted to set the Muslims up against the Croats, and those were the vestiges of the State Security Service in the former Yugoslavia, because it was impossible to target precisely the Croatian part of town and the Bosniak part of town from their positions at Kupres without having reconnaissance work. I don't think their crews were well -- sufficiently well trained to be able to target places just looking at maps, so reconnaissance work was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And I'd like to refer to another case that bears that out, the case of Mr. Tole, Chief of the Main Staff, later on his arrival in Vakuf and up at the front-line. And how did it come about that he was captured in Bugojno in the way that he was?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, General Zarko Tole arrived in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje at the beginning of May in 1992, and in the Radusa Hotel he held a joint meeting with 25 representatives of the Bosniak people and 25 representatives of the Croatian people, mostly key figures in the management of the Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje municipality, among whom were we, the commanders. And at that meeting, he offered up a proposal. He said that together we should advance towards the Army of Republika Srpska and set up units together, and that his mandate was -- and that he had reached an agreement whereby he would be the commander of this newly-established command. I have to say that we all accepted this proposal, and when the meeting was over, both the Croats and Bosniaks welcomed this with general applause. And two or three days later after the meeting was held, in Bugojno, in unexplained circumstances, General Zarko Tole was captured by the Army of Republika Srpska, or he was handed over to the Army of Republika Srpska. Anyway, they used him as a human shield, and they managed to pull out of Bugojno and advance to Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And how long did Zarko Tole spend in detention, in captivity?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I know the answer to that question, but more than a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, that's good. Now, the Prosecutor asked you several questions about when I was in the area in January, and he kept mentioning the territory of Uskoplje. So could you tell us, please, on what day was it that you were no longer able to leave Uskoplje and move towards Rama? What day were you not able to leave, and when were you able to leave Uskoplje and go to Rama?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, during my testimony here I said that on the 11th of January, after my deputy was captured, commander of the 1st Battalion and the commander of the 120th Battery, that members of the BH Army went down on their knees and tried to capture me and to place me under the supervision of the BH Army. And from that day onwards, that is to say, the 11th, I was no longer able to leave Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. No, 1993. I beg your pardon. And for as long as the HVO forces were not able to take control of the road between Gornji Vakuf, Uzricje, and Pidris, and the BH Army forces were in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But could I have been in Vakuf at all then, and did you ever -- could you ever meet me -- come across me in Rama?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was not able to go, except for meetings, I couldn't have seen you up there. And as I wasn't able to move around and move through that territory, you certainly couldn't have come to Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel asked you --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I apologise, but I don't think the interpretation was right there. Mr. Tokic, let me tell you how your answer was translated: "... as I was not able to go except for meetings, I couldn't have seen you up there." [Interpretation] From which it would follow that you were able to go to meetings. So could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I said that because of the blockade at the fire brigade tower, set up by the BH Army in the part of town where the majority population was Bosniak, I couldn't attend briefings to IZM Prozor, nor was I able to move around freely among my units, so I couldn't have seen General Praljak either at the forward command post, IZM, or in the Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje area because he couldn't move around either and go down there, except in an APC -- UNPROFOR APC. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Judge Trechsel asked you the following: When your soldiers returned from the front-line, when they would come back from the front-line and go home to farm the land and so on before they were called up again, in that kind of status when they were at home and when they, for example, stole a tractor or a cow or engaged in a brawl or anything like that, was it then your duty or the military police duty to intervene or was it the duty of the civilian police to intervene?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to answer that question, General, sir, because that person would be a soldier on furlough, but he would not be the subject of my interest, as a commander, because I would devote my attention to the front-line exclusively, whereas the civilian police and military police are there to secure public law and order in the town of Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje, outside the area where combat was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the last topic that I'd like to deal with is this: Tell me, please -- we heard mention of the fact that flying a Croatian flag, the national and historical flag or banner, could be taken to be provocation, so I have a few short questions for you. We saw where the front-line facing the Army Republika Srpska was. Now, do you remember that Paraga's -- Prijic's unit was ever up at the front-line facing the Army of Republika Srpska, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, as I dealt with most of the rotations, troop rotation, and when the BH Army -- we had consultations, the Green Berets were never engaged on Mount Radus. Now, whether they were deployed along some other line, I don't know, but I say with full responsibility that facing the Army of Republika Srpska up on Mount Radus, they were never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, purely from a military aspect, tell me this: When a joint army or friendly army, an army and troops to defend the country together, when they were stationed in the area of, say, Makljen and started digging, is that military provocation and a military threat? Is that tantamount to that?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Any engineering work on the territory for purposes of defence, outside of the official lines which threaten the Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje area, is considered to be a direct threat. That is to say, the people doing the digging are seen to be preparing themselves, whether through active defence or through an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember the problem, once again staying with relations and possible provocations and so on, when before the fall of Jajce the HVO unit set out to assist the unit led by Prkacin, what happened to the unit, and was it logical that this HVO unit was not able to go to Jajce as reinforcement, and were there military provocations and the clear sign of anything? Could you explain that to us a little, please?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I personally received an order telling me to escort the unit through my territory, through my area of responsibility, and that I should do that by maintaining communication with the BH Army and HVO Bugojno. And I agreed on this with the Commander Senad Dautovic on the BH Army side and Zdravko Babic on the HVO side. And at Ravno Rostovo, where I sent my military policemen - I wasn't there myself, personally - to the Mujahedin camp, of course, it's a ski area today, anyway, everybody was expelled, was taken out of the motor vehicles. They had to put their hands up in the air. There were two hours of negotiation, and Zdravko Babic arrived in the area, and Senad Dautovic. The Senad Dautovic unit was sent back without being given permission to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When a joint army is unable to pass through joint territory, is that a kind of occupation? Would that be a sort of occupation of that territory, and would you consider the other army to be hostile and an enemy army?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all event, this unit at that same location -- well, that's where Colonel Miro Andric was taken prisoner. He was stripped, all his possessions confiscated, and sent back to Bugojno. So that is a threat, first of all, to Croats in Central Bosnia, that they are not welcome there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And now my last question relates to something that the Prosecutor asked you, and it is this: Units who came into the Uskoplje area from outside, did they upset the BH Army side? Well, can you tell me whether those units came in before the beginning of the conflict, to provoke a conflict, or once the conflict had been going on for many days already?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, the conflict in Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje started on the 11th of January, and regardless of all the efforts made by the negotiators, it went on continuously until the 25th of January, 1993, with more or less intensity. And I said that the forces of the BH Army, through the 305th Jajce Brigade, upset the balance of peace or the balance of fear, whichever you'd like to call it, because after that we see the arrival of some military police, which gave rise to the amassment of forces both of the BH Army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO led its forces only once the conflict had broken out, except for those 60 military policemen who arrived on the 7th of January. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tokic. Thank you, Your Honours, for the time accorded me. I thank you all, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by cross Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, during Mr. Nozica's examination and the Prosecutor's questions you were shown your own statement, the statement given to this Defence team. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, that statement is 3D03712, for the record. You expressly answered -- or, rather, confirmed, asked by Ms. Nozica, that that was, indeed, your statement and that you stand by it, although it was just limited -- the question was just limited to an excerpt from your statement. What I'm going to ask you now is this: Did you give that statement of your own free will, on the basis of your own decision, to the investigators of the General Praljak Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I did give the statement of my own free will. And to demonstrate that, I initialled every single page and signed it. And I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions. Your Honours, we are going to place Mr. Tokic's statement on our IC list, although it was not our intention to use it because we thought that we could obtain everything we wanted to through the testimony. But since the other side raised the statement, then we'll put it on our IC list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning to you, Mr. Tokic, and everybody else in the courtroom. First of all, some information about the intentions of the Petkovic Defence with respect to additional questioning. We have a few short questions on two areas discussed during the cross-examination conducted by my learned friend Mr. Kruger, a short question from the cross-examination of the Stojic Defence on a topic that was touched upon in the examination-in-chief as well, and our redirect would be focused on the Stojic Defence team's about topics not encompassed during the examination-in-chief. We consider that the Trial Chamber, in allowing these questions to go -- to be asked, will also allow new topics to be broached, so we'd like to explain some of those topics. Let me tell you what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Ms. Alaburic, the Trial Chamber is very flexible. I was about to say even too tolerant. The redirect should have a direct connection, and this is stated by the Appeals Chamber, to the questions put by the Prosecutor, and the redirect must be closely linked to this. Remember that on such and such a page, the Prosecutor has stated this and that, and then you put your question. Redirect does not mean an examination-in-chief all over again. You must keep this in mind. I'm very surprised that you come back with a whole series of documents. If these documents have something to do with Mr. Kruger's questions, fine. Otherwise, no, this is not an examination-in-chief. You should have put your questions during the examination-in-chief. So please abide by the procedure. I will only listen to those questions which have a direct connection with what Mr. Kruger has said and with what the Judges have said. This is what Mr. Praljak has done. We have scrutinised all this, we have looked at the questions he raised, and the same applies to you. There is no question of addressing a new topic. I hope this is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have completely misunderstood me. Not a single of my questions is going to refer to any of the subjects that were not raised during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, needless to make a statement. Just put your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to correct the transcript. Were not raised during examination-in-chief, but rather during cross-examination, primarily by Bruno Stojic's Defence team, and the General Petkovic's Defence team is not going to use even as much time as General Praljak consumed for his redirect. And I honestly don't understand why this attempt on my part to explain to you the structure of redirect provoked such a reaction. I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Chamber and to my learned friend. I would just like to say that the cross-examination of the Bruno Stojic's Defence team went beyond the limits of direct -- examination-in-chief. I can only surmise that this refers to parts of cross-examination of Stojic's Defence, and I would like to say that none of the questions raised were outside of the documents put to Mr. Tokic. The majority of questioning referred to document 3D796, which Mr. Praljak showed during direct examination and again today during redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, put your questions, and we will see whether this is part of the scope of questions or not. Further re-examination by Ms. Alaburic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tokic, yesterday, in response to the questions put by my learned friend Mr. Kruger on page 68 of the record, the question was whether Gornji Vakuf could have been part of the Herceg-Bosna in view of the fact that the majority of population were Muslims, my question to you, Mr. Tokic, is as follows: According to the Vance-Owen Plan, Gornji Vakuf was allocated to what we simply call the Croatian province?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Vance-Owen Plan, Gornji Vakuf-Uskoplje was supposed to become part of the Croatian province.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You spoke about war prisoners when you were asked by my learned friend the Prosecutor, the prisoners who were housed in a factory. Can you tell us for how long these prisoners were kept in this factory?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war prisoners housed in this factory remained there until the end of combat operations, when conditions were ripe for them to return to the areas where they had been living before the conflict started. Therefore, I would say about 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokic, were the war prisoners released immediately after the combat operations or were some of them transferred to Prozor? Can you clarify this a little bit more? I'm talking solely about war -- prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about the POWs from the BH Army, those for whom evidence was collected that indicated that they should be subjected to additional investigation, they were transferred to the area around Prozor, because I'm not sure about the specific location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Tokic, had you heard that one of the POWs named Hasan Behlo sustained bodily injury while in captivity?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard about that incident. I was informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, after the cessation of combat operations, was any proceeding instituted against the person who inflicted these injuries on Mr. Behlo?

utterances.speaker: ZRINKO TOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The military police and the Security Department instituted proceedings against members of -- a member of HOS. I think that his name was Kristo, last name, probably Stipo, first name, and I'm quite sure that the proceedings were set in motion, and this prisoner was taken care of in the infirmary of the 1st Battalion and an ambulance took him to Rumboci for further treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
